Bhoja was a follower of the Śaiva tradition of Hinduism, and he was deeply devoted to Lord Śiva. He built numerous temples and performed several religious ceremonies to honour the deity.

In addition to his scholarly pursuits, Bhoja was also a skilled warrior and an able ruler. He expanded his Kingdom through conquests and alliances and was respected and feared by his contemporaries.

However, towards the end of his reign, his kingdom faced several challenges, including invasions from neighbouring states and internal strife. Bhoja’s health also deteriorated, and he eventually passed away in the year 1055 CE.

Despite the challenges he faced in his later years, Rāja Bhoja’s legacy as a scholar and patron of art and literature has endured over the centuries. His writings and patronage have influenced subsequent generations of writers and scholars, and he is remembered as one of the most prominent figures of the Paramara dynasty.
Contribution of the poet to the Sanskrit: Bhoja made significant contributions to classical Sanskrit literature by promoting and preserving the intellectual and cultural traditions of ancient India. His works spanned a wide range of fields, including poetry, philosophy, history, science, and law. Bhoja's poetry is considered to be among the finest examples of Sanskrit literature and his treatises on aesthetics, language, and philosophy provided critical insights into the nature and purpose of literature and language. Additionally, his work on science and technology provided insights into the technological advancements of medieval India and the practical applications of scientific knowledge. In a nutshell, Bhoja's contribution to Classical Sanskrit literature reflects his deep interest in exploring the connections between different fields of knowledge and his efforts to synthesize their insights into a coherent whole.

Title: Bilhaṇa
Life of the Poet:
Bilhaṇa is a renowned Sanskrit poet who lived in India during the 11th century AD. He was born in the town of Warangal, which is located in present-day Telangana state in South India. Bilhaṇa was a Kshatriya caste member, traditionally associated with the warrior class in Hindu society.
Bilhaṇa is most famous for his three significant works of poetry: Vikramāṇkadevacaritam, Karṇasundarī, and Caurapañcāśikā. Vikramāṇkadevacaritam is a long narrative poem that tells the story of the legendary king Vikramāditya, while Karṇasundarī is a romantic tale of a young woman named Karṇasundarī and her lover Candrāpīḍa. Caurapañcāśikā is a collection of fifty stanzas that explore the nature of love and desire.
In addition to his poetry, Bilhaṇa was known for his warrior and military commander skills. He served as a general in the army of the Kalyāṇī Chālukya dynasty, which ruled over parts of South India during the 11th century. Bilhaṇa's military exploits are celebrated in the Vikramāṇkadevacaritam, which includes vivid descriptions of battles and warfare.
Despite his success as a poet and warrior, Bilhaṇa faced significant challenges in his personal life. According to some accounts, he was forced to flee Warangal after his father was killed in a political dispute. Bilhaṇa eventually found refuge at the court of the Kalyāṇī Chālukya king Vikramāditya VI, where he could pursue his poetic and military ambitions.
Bilhaṇa's life and works are essential for their insights into the culture and society of medieval India. His poetry reflects the values and beliefs of his time, including the importance of love, honour, and courage in both personal and political life. Today, Bilhaṇa is remembered as one of the greatest Sanskrit poets of the medieval period, and his works continue to be studied and admired by scholars and readers worldwide.
Contribution of the poet to the Sanskrit:
Bilhaṇa made several significant contributions to Sanskrit literature during his lifetime. His most notable works, Vikramāṇkadevacaritam, Karṇasundarī, and Caurapañcāśikā, are all highly regarded for their literary merit, unique style, and thematic depth.
Vikramāṇkadevacaritam, for example, is a masterpiece of courtly poetry and is widely considered one of the greatest works of Sanskrit literature. Its use of the narrative framework is unique, allowing for a complex interweaving of multiple storylines and characters. Bilhaṇa's lyrical and poetic language, combined with his vivid descriptions of landscapes and textures, makes the work an enduring masterpiece of Indian literature.
Karṇasundarī is also a significant work in Sanskrit literature and is notable for its use of the Śṛṅgāra rasa, or the sentiment of love, as its central theme. The poem explores the protagonist's emotional journey, Karṇasundarī, as she falls in love with a young warrior. 
Finally, Caurapañcāśikā is an essential contribution to the genre of romantic poetry and is notable for its use of the thief as its narrator and protagonist. Bilhaṇa's portrayal of the thief as a charming and witty character, who uses his skills to win the heart of his beloved, is a unique and refreshing take on the theme of love and desire.
In summary, Bilhaṇa's contributions to Sanskrit literature have had a lasting impact on Indian culture and continue to be celebrated and studied.

Title: Hanumakavi
Life of the Poet:
The attribution of the Hanumānāṭaka or Mahānāṭaka to a single author is ambiguous due to conflicting information from various sources. Poets such as Damodaramiśra and Madhusūdanamiśra mention different kings in the text, which adds to the confusion. According to Damodaramiśra, Bhoja Rāja, who lived in the 11th century, is referred to in the play, while Madhusūdanamiśra mentions a king named Vikrama who lived in the 12th century.
It is worth noting that Lakṣmaṇasena was also known by the name Vikramāditya. This speculation is supported by certain verses in Dyōyi’s Pavanadūta:
         khyāto yaśca śrutidhāratayā vikramādityaghoṣṭhi |
vidyābhartuḥ khalu vararucirasasada pratiṣṭhām ||
It is likely that the poets who mentioned these kings in the text lived during the same timeline. Despite efforts to uncover the identity and origin of Hanumānkavi, there remains a significant lack of information on the subject. Similarly, the origins and authorship of these plays are still shrouded in mystery, leaving a significant gap in our understanding of their history.

Title: Kriṣṇamiśra
Life of the Poet:
Kriṣṇamiśra was a prominent Sanskrit poet of the 11th century, who composed works in a variety of genres including poetry, drama, and philosophy. Kriṣṇamiśra's literary output was prolific, and his works are known for their complex wordplay, vivid descriptions, and poetic language. One of his most famous works is the play Prabōdhācāndrōdaya, which combines elements of Hindu mythology, philosophy, and romance. The play has ten acts and is known for its intricate plot and literary style. Kriṣṇamiśra was an ascetic belonging to Hansa order of the Advaita School and had many disciplines.
Contribution of the poet to the Sanskrit: Kṛṣṇamiśra was a prolific writer and scholar who made significant contributions to classical Sanskrit literature. In addition to Prabodhacandrodaya, he also wrote several other plays. Kṛṣṇamiśra was also a noted poet, who wrote numerous works in a variety of genres, including kāvya, gadya, and Campū. His poetry is characterized by its intricate language, skilful use of imagery, and exploration of both traditional and contemporary themes. Kṛṣṇamiśra was also a respected scholar and commentator, who wrote extensive commentaries on the works of earlier Sanskrit authors, such as Kāḷidāsa and Bhāsa. Overall, Kriṣṇamiśra’s contributions to classical Sanskrit literature were wide-ranging and influential, and helped to shape the literary and intellectual landscape of medieval India.

Title: Kṣemendra
Life of the Poet: Kṣemendra is a significant figure in the history of Sanskrit literature, not just poetry. He had a mastermind and a wide range of interests and wrote several treatises on various subjects. He is genuinely referred to as a polymath. Nineteen years later we hear from him again in the prelude to Śrīvara where his prologue has been dated to his Sanskrit translation of Jāmi’s Persian Yusof o Zoleykhā, titled ‘Kathākautukam’ - as April 18, 1505. The sudden interruption of Śrīvara’s Jain- Rājataraṅgiṇī, coinciding with the transition of power in 1486, could be associated with his removal from the position of court biographer. His accounts, the Jaina- and Rājataraṅgiṇīs, written as an eyewitness, are characterised by remarkably detailed density that hardly leaves out any aspect of his contemporary horizon of observation and reflection on everyday Kashmiri culture, court life, politics, religion, and society. The consolidation of the religious and political influence of a group of Sayyids, who had migrated from Baihaq in Iran under earlier Śāhmīrī Sulṭāns such as Sikandar, and the dynamics triggered by their attempts under Hasan Śāh and Maḥmūd Śāh to participate in the reign, culminated in a devastating civil war between factions of indigenous Kashmiris (kāśmīrika) and the immigrants from abroad (paradeśīya, vaideśika). These events are of research interest for tracing the historical ramifications of the Islamisation process in Kāśmīr. In terms of richness of detail of everyday culture including its material aspects, Śrīvara’s work is the most abundant source on Indo-Persian rule in early modern India and the living conditions under omnipresent threats of famines, natural disasters, and warfare. But the reflection of these histories in Sanskrit poetry needs more notice.
 Kathākautukam was described by the Austrian scholar and historian of Sanskrit M Winternitz as an adaptation rather than translation of Jami’s poem. In his words it is an “amalgamation of the Hebrew story, Persian romantic ballad and the Indian Siva cult.” In this description he omitted mention of another important contributory source, namely, Islam.  
The Sanskrit poem’s narrative also includes a list of names – like Adam – taken from Jami and the Semite scriptures. Yakub and Yusuf are identifiable and mentioned as such in this translation. Others remain in the original forms in which they occur in the Sanskrit text. Only one, Ajajamesra, was rendered as Mesra-born. Bearing in mind its accompanying reference to a river, Mesra is obviously Egypt, and Nila the River Nile.
The Sanskrit text also has references to various divinities and heroes from Indian mythology. All their names are given in the original form. The principal mention in Kathākautukam is that of the great god Śiva, also presented in his cosmic aspect, and referred to by the poet with various synonyms, many of which are well-known.
 Śrīvara uses both Indian and Semite origin in the narrative sequences of the work. They also make evident its composite cultural background. A good example of this is in the narration of chapter 10, of the boy Yusuf’s abandonment in a forest and his rescue from a well with the help of the god Śankara and the angel Gabriel. There are several others, which a brief reading would easily locate. 
Śrīvara received the patronage of three successive rulers, Zainulabidin, his son Hyder Śāh and grandson Hasan Śāh, in the fifteenth century. Dr. Nagarajan notes that this coincided with the brief rule of Sultans, who were independent of the Delhi Sultanate and showed great interest in Vālmīki Ramayana, Yogavāsiṣṭha, Bṛhatkathā, Purāṇas  and Dharmaśāstra.
